notes: Short sentencing appeal on section 116 licence recall credit; principles from Stocker and Teasdale are clearly applied.

enrichment.short_title: Section 116 recall: credit for time on revoked licence
key_facts: Francis Healy pleaded guilty to handling stolen goods and received 15 months consecutive to 537 days under section 116 for breach of licence.
He had been released on licence from a 4½-year sentence about six weeks before further offending and spent 81 days in custody after licence revocation before sentencing.
The sentencing judge was not told about the 81-day period served under revoked licence status.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against sentence for handling stolen goods and section 116 recall term.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed in part; section 116 term reduced from 537 days to 375 days after doubling the 81 days served and deducting from the maximum.
enrichment.ratio: Where an offender is returned to custody under section 116 following revocation of licence under section 39, the court must allow appropriate credit for time spent in custody after revocation; for short-term prisoners the conventional approach is to double that period and deduct it from the section 116 maximum.
legal_issues: Whether credit should be given for 81 days served after licence revocation
How Stocker and Teasdale apply to section 116 calculations
Whether the overall 15-month handling sentence was excessive
linked_authorities: R v Stocker [2003] 2 Cr App R (S) 54
R v Teasdale [2004] 1 Cr App R (S) 6

notes: Tenby harbour parking judicial review; improper purpose and property-rights grounds are comprehensively analysed.

enrichment.short_title: Tenby harbour parking directions ultra vires challenge
key_facts: Pembrokeshire County Council adopted harbour byelaw-based parking directions covering Castle Terrace outside the Richards' Tenby property.
The owners challenged the Directions as outside harbour operational powers, unreasonable, and infringing Article 1 Protocol 1 rights.
Moses J dismissed the claim; the owners appealed on vires, irrationality, and private property grounds.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from judicial review refusing to quash Tenby Harbour vehicle-use Directions 2003.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed on two grounds: the stated reasons showed an improper non-harbour purpose, and the council failed to consider that the Directions might invade private property rights on Castle Terrace without compensation.
enrichment.ratio: Parking directions made under harbour legislation must pursue harbour operational purposes reflected in the Harbours Act 1964; where contemporaneous reasons show primary concern with town-centre congestion and pedestrian safety, later officer evidence cannot rewrite an ultra vires decision, and private-property impacts on non-highway land must be considered before restricting parking.
legal_issues: Whether the Directions were made for a harbour operational purpose
Whether section 44(3) precludes challenging byelaws made under an ultra vires harbour revision order
Whether post-decision evidence may explain or alter stated reasons
Whether the council failed to consider private property rights over Castle Terrace

notes: Procedural refusal of multiple charging-order and legal-aid applications; Pitchers J findings treated as unarguable.

enrichment.short_title: Charging order appeal and ancillary applications refused
key_facts: Ayobiojo, a prisoner, sought permission to appeal Pitchers J's order making a final charging order over jointly owned property after Master Ungley discharged an interim order.
Pitchers J found a forged divorce petition had been produced and that a charging order should stand even if the transfer intention were genuine.
The applicant made numerous further applications including legal aid, production orders, contempt against solicitors, and adjournment by video link.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Applications for permission to appeal and multiple ancillary applications heard in the applicant's absence after he refused to use a video link.
enrichment.outcome: All applications refused; no arguable ground to disturb Pitchers J's charging-order decision; legal aid and adjournment applications rejected.
enrichment.ratio: A second appeal against clear findings that a document was forged and that Austin-Fell principles supported a charging order is not arguable; Article 6 does not require legal aid unless effective access to court would otherwise be denied, and a litigant who declines procedural opportunities cannot later complain of unfairness.
legal_issues: Whether Pitchers J erred in finding the divorce petition forged
Whether the applicant was entitled to legal representation or a production order
Whether Article 6 and equality of arms required different procedure
Whether solicitors committed contempt by obtaining registry access under court order

Perotti v Collyer-Bristow [2003] EWCA Civ 1521

notes: Major brain-injury quantum appeal; Social Security Recovery of Benefits Act and receiver issues are detailed.

enrichment.short_title: Severe brain injury damages: care regime and benefits
key_facts: Claimant Eagle suffered catastrophic brain injury when knocked down in 1989; liability trial in 2002 apportioned contributory negligence at 40%.
Cooke J awarded about £1.5m damages, principally for a privately funded care regime at £66,000 per year and new accommodation.
Both parties appealed on care costs, Kemsley rehabilitation, benefits, receiver fees, panel brokers, interest, and miscellaneous heads of loss.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal and cross-appeal against assessment of damages following liability trial in Eagle v Chambers.
enrichment.outcome: Mixed result: mobility allowance/Motability mitigation rejected; NHS/Social Services item deductions restored for laundry, chiropody and pads; cleaning award restored; Kemsley costs and most other reductions upheld; panel brokers fees refused (majority).
enrichment.ratio: Section 17 of the 1997 Act requires listed benefits to be disregarded in assessing damages, so a claimant cannot be required to use mobility allowance to fund a cheaper Motability scheme; where a private care regime is ordered, defendants must prove NHS or social-services provision of ancillary items, and late appellate challenges to expert care costings not raised at trial will generally fail.
legal_issues: Whether privately funded full-time care rather than social-services top-up was recoverable
Whether section 17 precludes requiring use of mobility allowance to mitigate transport costs
Whether panel brokers fees are recoverable for Court of Protection patients
Whether income support wrongly deducted and whether interest should be reduced for litigation delay

notes: Workplace Regulations trip claim; Marks & Spencer suitability approach applied and contributory negligence upheld.

enrichment.short_title: Prison Rapiscan step: workplace floor suitability appeal
key_facts: Mrs Lowles, a prison instructional officer, tripped on a 2-inch unmarked step at the top of a covered ramp into a Rapiscan portacabin at HMP Leeds.
A red 'PLEASE MIND THE STEP' notice was present; she was talking to a colleague and not concentrating when the inner door was opened.
The recorder found breach of regulation 12 and common-law negligence but apportioned 50% contributory negligence.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Home Office appeal and claimant cross-appeal from recorder's liability and contributory negligence findings.
enrichment.outcome: Both appeal and cross-appeal dismissed; 2-inch step at ramp top was unsuitable and a relevant obstruction despite warning sign; 50% contributory negligence not disturbed.
enrichment.ratio: Under regulation 12, floor suitability requires a contextual health-and-safety assessment of risk before the accident, not automatic liability from any trip; an unexpected intermediate step at a ramp top may be unsuitable and an obstruction even with a warning sign, while claimant inattention does not eliminate liability but supports contributory negligence.
legal_issues: Whether the step breached regulation 12(1) and (3)
Correct approach after Marks & Spencer v Palmer to floor suitability
Whether a warning sign discharged the employer's duty
Whether 50% contributory negligence was wrong
linked_authorities: Marks & Spencer plc v Palmer [2001] EWCA Civ 1528
Assicurazioni Generali SpA v Arab Insurance Group [2002] EWCA Civ 1642

notes: NNDR liability order set-aside challenge; Pleroma inherent jurisdiction limits applied to late reopening.

enrichment.short_title: Magistrates set aside stale NNDR liability orders

statutes_considered.title: Non-Domestic Rating (Collection and Enforcement) (Local Lists) Regulations 1989

key_facts: Brighton and Hove Council obtained three NNDR liability orders against Mr Hamdan in 1996-1997 totalling £5,734.55 for a Hove property he disputed occupying.
After a 2002 statutory demand and bankruptcy petition, Hamdan applied in 2003 to set aside the orders claiming the property was never an office unit.
Lay justices set aside all three orders; the council sought judicial review.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of magistrates' decision to set aside historic business-rates liability orders.
enrichment.outcome: Claim granted; magistrates exceeded their limited inherent jurisdiction to reopen liability orders where there was no substantial procedural defect and the application was not prompt.
enrichment.ratio: Following Liverpool City Council v Pleroma, magistrates may set aside a liability order only in exceptional cases where there is a genuine arguable liability dispute plus a substantial procedural error and a prompt application; a general 'interests of justice' test cannot justify reopening orders years later after the debtor knew of proceedings.
legal_issues: Whether judicial review or case stated was the proper challenge route
Whether magistrates had power to set aside the liability orders
Whether service defects or substantive dispute justified reopening
Whether the application was made promptly enough

notes: Called-in Ellesmere mixed-use refusal; section 54A reasoning adequate though supermarket impact explanation weak.

enrichment.short_title: Ellesmere Dairy Crest planning refusal challenge

statutes_considered.title: Town and Country Planning (Environmental Impact Assessment) (England and Wales) Regulations 1999

key_facts: Burbury Investments sought outline permission for a factory outlet centre, supermarket, hotel, caravan park and 186 homes on the former Dairy Crest site at Ellesmere.
An inspector recommended grant after a called-in inquiry; the Secretary of State refused, treating the factory outlet as unacceptable retail development under PPG6 and PPG13.
The claimant challenged the decision under section 288, including alleged section 54A failures and inadequate reasons on foodstore impact.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Section 288 statutory challenge to Secretary of State refusal of called-in outline planning application.
enrichment.outcome: Challenge dismissed; permission to appeal refused. Factory outlet refusal upheld; housing prematurity and transport reasoning defects did not materially prejudice the claimant.
enrichment.ratio: Under section 54A a decision-maker need not evaluate every development-plan policy separately if the substance of plan-related considerations is addressed; a large factory outlet in a small market town with poor public transport may outweigh plan allocation where PPG6 as clarified requires demonstrated need, but unexplained inconsistency with an earlier minded-to-grant decision on supermarket impact is a reasons defect that may not vitiate the whole decision if the FOC element is fundamentally objectionable.
legal_issues: Whether the Secretary of State complied with section 54A in weighing development-plan policies
Whether the factory outlet was properly treated as retail rather than tourism
Whether housing element was prematurely determined
Whether inadequate reasons on foodstore impact and linked trips invalidated the decision

notes: Brussels II forum dispute; Family Law Act construction clarified but practical occupation relief refused.

enrichment.short_title: Family Law Act occupation order after tenancy ended
key_facts: Affluent divorcing couple disputed occupation of leased Thurloe Square after the husband gave notice ending the tenancy.
French and English divorce proceedings competed; a French court later declined jurisdiction on habitual residence.
The wife sought Family Law Act occupation orders and financial relief while the husband's stay application remained unresolved.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from Singer J's refusal of Family Law Act occupation order applications pending cross-border divorce litigation.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed with 50% costs to the husband; court differed from Singer J on section 30/33 construction but refused practical occupation relief after tenancy termination.
enrichment.ratio: Matrimonial home rights under section 30 are not permanently extinguished merely because a qualifying contractual tenancy ends and a new one is later acquired; section 33 may apply where entitlement is by contract or matrimonial home rights, but a four-day rent-free licence or ordering the husband to obtain a new lease is too insubstantial to found occupation relief in the circumstances.
legal_issues: Whether section 33 applies after termination of the husband's contractual tenancy
Whether the court could require the husband to withdraw a notice to quit or take a new lease under section 37
Interaction of Brussels II with English financial and occupation remedies
Whether a temporary licence from landlords created contractual occupation rights
linked_authorities: Wermuth v Wermuth [2003] 1 WLR 942

confidence.notes: Statutory construction point is clear though overall relief refused. Competing jurisdiction facts evolved during hearing.

notes: Costs judgment following NNDR liability-order JR; Calderbank-style offer and no-order outcome are clear.

enrichment.short_title: NNDR JR costs after rejected settlement offer
key_facts: These were costs applications following Brighton Council's successful judicial review of magistrates setting aside NNDR liability orders against Mr Hamdan.
Total costs claimed by the council exceeded the rates debt; Mr Hamdan had not been properly served for an earlier consent hearing.
On 28 January 2004 Hamdan's solicitors proposed setting aside the justices' order and allowing magistrates to reconsider; the council never responded.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Costs applications after judgment in related judicial review proceedings.
enrichment.outcome: No order as to costs; substantive order quashed the magistrates' decision and required reconsideration in light of the main judgment.
enrichment.ratio: Where a litigant makes a sensible without-prejudice offer to settle proceedings that is ignored, and the claimant's costs were excessive or hearings were necessitated by poor service and adjournments, justice may be done by making no order for costs despite the claimant's substantive success.
legal_issues: Who should pay costs of three High Court hearings in the judicial review
Effect of the council's failure to respond to Hamdan's settlement proposal
Whether the council's costs were disproportionate to the sum in dispute

notes: Long-delayed banking trial; guarantee/mortgage and account retrial issues are comprehensively reviewed.

enrichment.short_title: Habib Bank fraud trial: guarantee and accounts appeal
key_facts: Habib Bank sued Mr Iqbal on a guarantee and mortgage securing alleged debts of Streed and Streed UK; Mrs Iqbal counterclaimed for wrongful account debits after branch manager Mr Butt's parallel-banking fraud.
Judge Kershaw delivered judgment in instalments after extreme delay following a 2001-2002 trial.
The judge held the guarantee secured only a $146,000 Streed UK letter-of-credit facility, the mortgage did not bind Mr Iqbal personally, and Mrs Iqbal's account claims required further trial.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Bank appeal with permission against Mercantile List judgment in consolidated guarantee and wrongful-debit actions.
enrichment.outcome: Bank's appeal on guarantee and mortgage dismissed; appeal in Mrs Iqbal's action allowed with retrial ordered before a different judge; Mr Iqbal entitled to release of the Dixon Mill mortgage.
enrichment.ratio: Excessive delay and provisional Scott-schedule findings without adequate reasons may render account findings unsafe; a standard guarantee naming Streed UK and secured by Streed's dollar deposit limits liability to that facility, and estoppel by convention cannot rewrite a mortgage without proved common assumption.
legal_issues: Construction and rectification of Mr Iqbal's guarantee
Whether estoppel made the mortgage secure company indebtedness
Whether delayed judgment findings on account balances were safe
Effect of Mr Butt's parallel banking on proof of account balances
linked_authorities: Cobham v Frett [2001] 1 WLR 1775
Amalgamated Property Co v Texas Bank [1982] QB 84
